# Task-Fidelity Harness

The widget gauntlet checks whether each tool behaves. The task-fidelity harness
asks a different question: did the whole run deliver what the user asked for?
It drives complete agentic runs against generic fixture sites. It then measures
the outcome from the run's own artifacts, an independent server-side request
log, and browser-reported fixture form state held by the server.

The harness has two tiers, and both use the same fixture sites:

| Tier          | Entry point                             | Drives the run with                   | Gates CI |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------- |
| Deterministic | `e2e/task-fidelity.spec.ts` (`@no-llm`) | A scripted agent playing a fixed plan | Yes      |
| Agentic       | `pnpm eval:tasks`                       | A real model, three runs per scenario | Never    |

This feature is for maintainers. It adds no `yantra` command and changes no run
artifact format. The scorecard it writes is a versioned, dev-only harness file.
The production code changes are two seams, and neither does anything unless a
caller uses it. For how the harness fits the runtime (the environment-leaves
seam and the audit projection), see
[architecture: task-fidelity harness](../architecture.md#task-fidelity-harness)
and
[default environment composition and leaves](../architecture.md#default-environment-composition-and-leaves).

## What It Does

### Runs production code with only the leaves swapped

Every scenario runs through `runScenario` in `e2e/task-fidelity/runner.ts`.
That function calls the real `runAgenticTask()` with the production default
environment composer. The harness swaps only leaf dependencies, through
`AgenticTaskDependencies.environmentLeaves`:

- the HTTP transport is `mappedRequestFn`;
- the browser factory wraps the production `createSelectedBrowserProvider` in
  `hostMappedBrowserProvider`;
- the search resolver returns the scripted search provider;
- the ethics config is `defaultEthicsConfig`, so robots rules are honored;
- the search config is `DEFAULT_SEARCH_CONFIG`; and
- the blocklist is empty.

The deterministic tier also swaps in an in-memory keychain that holds one
planted canary secret. The agentic tier keeps the real keychain, because the
model credentials live there.

Everything built on top of those leaves is production code: the ethics gate,
the hybrid fetcher, the browser controller, the publisher, URL policy, budgets,
the sanitizer, consent, and audit recording. A harness measurement therefore
follows the composer when a later feature rewires it.

Each run also has these fixed settings:

- The command profile comes from
  `resolveCommandTaskProfile(scenario.command, { browse: scenario.browse ?? true })`.
  The catalog is decided by the scenario alone: a `research` scenario gets the
  read-only browser tools, as the product default does, unless it sets
  `browse: false`. Nothing in the environment can change the catalog, so a
  developer's shell cannot change a measurement.
- The location grant is on. The screenshots grant is off unless the scenario
  sets `visionAssist: true`; then the grant is on and the scripted model is
  treated as image-capable, so `browser_screenshot` is registered. Otherwise
  the scripted model is text-only. The local `browser_capture` needs neither,
  so every `do` scenario has it unless the scenario sets
  `screenshotsSuppressed: true`, which runs as `--no-screenshots` would and
  removes both capture tools.
- `urlPolicyConfig` allows plain HTTP (`requireHttps: false`).
- A silent, non-interactive connector denies every confirmation request and
  counts how many it received.
- A recording rank sink captures every domain rank signal.
- In the deterministic tier, the run's budget clock is real time plus whatever
  the script's `advance-clock` steps have added, so a script can cross the
  exploration wind-down without waiting for it.

The deterministic tier runs under a temporary `YANTRA_HOME` and calls
`resetPathCache()` before and after. No developer state leaks into a run, and no
run writes into the developer's home. The agentic tier keeps the developer's
home, so the CLI's model configuration and credentials apply. Its run
directories still go under the output directory.

### Hosts every fixture under its own reserved hostname

Each fixture site is served at `<name>.yantra.test`, over both `http://` and
`https://`. RFC 2606 reserves `.test`, so these names can never resolve
publicly. Distinct hostnames matter: host budgets, required-source checks, and
ranking all key off the hostname. If every fixture shared `127.0.0.1`, source
fidelity would always pass.

One loopback server, `serveTaskSites()`, answers for every site. It listens on
one ephemeral port and answers both schemes there, the way a real site answers
on ports 80 and 443. It reads the first byte of each connection: a TLS
handshake goes to an HTTPS server, and anything else goes to a plain HTTP
server. The TLS certificate comes from `fixtures/tls.ts`. It is a self-signed
ECDSA P-256 certificate for `*.yantra.test`, generated in memory once per
process, so no private key is committed. The server routes each request by its
`Host` header:

- Every fixture host serves `User-agent: *` / `Allow: /` at `/robots.txt`.
- Every site except `challenge-interstitial` serves a home page at `/` that
  links to the site's main pages. `article` also serves `/guides` and `/about`.
- `test-form` also answers its submit beacon, `/apply/submit-event`, with an
  empty 204.
- `challenge-interstitial` challenges every page, like a real bot wall: the
  `small` variant at its own path, and the `large-main` variant everywhere else.
- On every other site, an unknown path gets a 404, and so does an unknown host.
- Responses are sent with `cache-control: no-store`.

The fixtures behave like real sites in these respects for a measured reason. A
first agentic run was discarded because it measured harness defects instead of
the pipeline: models reached for `https://`, opened bare hosts, and searched by
site name, and the fixtures then served plain HTTP only, had no home pages, and
matched only narrow search queries. The implementation notes in
`.spec-lite/features/FEAT-049-task_fidelity_harness/spec.md` record the
details.

The server keeps its own request log. Each entry records:

- arrival order;
- the `scheme`, `http` or `https`;
- host, path, query, and method;
- `userAgentClass`: `browser` for a Chrome user agent, `http` otherwise;
- a `robots` flag; and
- the response status and arrival time.

The log covers ordinary requests, including robots requests and 404s. Fixture
state posts to `/__fixture/state` are collected separately in `stateLog()` and
never enter the request log. The harness counts network fetches from the request
log, independently of anything the run reports about itself, without counting
its form-state measurement traffic.

Both transports map fixture hosts to the server, and both fail closed:

| Transport | Mapping                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Anything else                                                                                                                                                                            |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| HTTP      | `mappedRequestFn(port, egress)` is `HttpFetcher`'s `requestFn`. It connects a `*.yantra.test` target to `127.0.0.1:<port>` and keeps the original `Host` header. An `https:` fixture URL is served by the same loopback server over plain HTTP, because TLS changes nothing this tier observes.                                                                                                                               | A host that is neither a fixture host nor loopback is rejected with `HarnessEgressError` and recorded in an `EgressLog`. Any other non-`http:` URL is rejected with `HarnessSetupError`. |
| Chrome    | `hostMappedBrowserProvider(inner, port, counter)` appends `--host-resolver-rules=EXCLUDE localhost,MAP *.yantra.test 127.0.0.1:<port>,MAP * ~NOTFOUND` and `--ignore-certificate-errors` to `extraArgs` on every launch. Only the harness's Chrome gets that flag, and because every other name fails to resolve, it cannot reach a real site. It delegates every other member unchanged and keeps the inner provider's type. | Every other name fails to resolve.                                                                                                                                                       |

The production `HttpFetcher` turns any transport throw into a generic network
error, so the egress log is what makes a refusal visible. Every scenario
asserts the log is empty. The browser decorator counts successful launches in a
`LaunchCounter` shared by every provider in the run. Like the request log, it
measures from outside the code under test, so measuring adds no page read,
fetch, or launch to the run.

### Serves a nine-pattern fixture gallery

All listing pages render from one 14-item fictional inventory in
`fixtures/inventory.ts`. The ground truth is `truthRows()`, which derives from
the same array, so a page cannot show a value the truth does not hold.

- Colors appear only on detail pages, so a complete answer has to follow detail
  links.
- Some items deliberately fail exactly one of the canonical filters (new, 2026,
  `Summit` trim, `AWD`). A delivered row from one of them is a measurable
  violation, not a near miss.
- Six cards make one listing page.

| Site                      | Generic pattern                                                                                                                           | Provenance                     |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `faceted-listing`         | Server-rendered cards with facet links, pagination links, and detail pages that hold the attributes the cards omit                        | run `20260925T130634Z`; G2, G3 |
| `structured-listing`      | Records that exist only as schema.org JSON-LD (`ItemList` of `Product` with nested `Offer` and seller `Organization`) behind a thin shell | G2                             |
| `client-rendered-listing` | Records injected by script after load into an empty shell: under 10 KB, an external script `src`, no `<main>` or `<article>`              | G2, G5                         |
| `challenge-interstitial`  | An HTTP 200 human-verification widget form in place of the content, with no listing data, in two variants                                 | run `20260925T130634Z`; G10    |
| `article`                 | A long-form article (about 1,500 words) with a byline and `datePublished` JSON-LD, inside site chrome                                     | G2                             |
| `multi-table`             | A specification page whose first table is an unrelated summary; the answer is in the second table                                         | G2                             |
| `test-form`               | A long single-page application form, larger than the observation cap, to be filled and not submitted                                      | run `20261014T023539Z`; G4     |
| `tall-page`               | A page far taller than the viewport, with a short form at the top and a labeled panel below the fold                                      | run `20261014T023539Z`; G7, G8 |
| `form-lab`                | Layout-matrix forms with independent field-state and submission measurement                                                               | G2, G8                         |

The first `faceted-listing` card is the G2 regression card. Its price is plain
text, while its title and seller are links.

The two challenge variants measure today's page-size heuristic for browser
escalation (G10) instead of relying on it:

- `small` is under 10 KB, has a script `src`, and has no semantic root. The
  hybrid fetcher escalates it to a browser render.
- `large-main` wraps the same widget in `<main>` and pads it past 10 KB. The
  fetcher does not escalate it. The site serves this variant at its own path
  and at every other path, including `/`.

The widget markers are generic widget vocabulary, a `data-sitekey` attribute and
a `captcha` token on a class, id, and name inside a `<form>`. No vendor or brand
appears.

`test-form` holds no truth rows. It serves two pages, each one `<form>` with a
typeless submit button named "Send application" and a `type="button"` control
named "Add another reference":

- `/apply` has more than 50 eligible controls: labeled text, email, telephone,
  password, URL, and date inputs, 32 numbered "Answer" inputs, native selects,
  a radio group in a `fieldset` with a `legend`, two checkboxes, and a text
  area. It also carries the controls an honest "fill every field" leaves
  alone: a disabled input, a read-only input, a file input, and a hidden
  input. Its buttons sit past the 50-element observation cap.
- `/quick-apply` has three text inputs and the same two buttons, all inside
  the observation cap.

`tall-page` also holds no truth rows. It exists so that "take a screenshot"
can mean three different things: the visible viewport, the whole scrollable
page, or one element outside the visible area. Every block has a fixed size and
the page has no margin, so the capture geometry follows from the source alone:

- `/report` is 9,000 px tall, which a full-page capture covers in three
  4,096 px tiles.
- `/report/long` is 30,000 px tall, more than six tiles, so a full-page capture
  can cover it only in part and must say so.
- Both pages have a form at the top with a "Your name" text field, an "Account
  password" password field, and a "Save draft" `type="button"` control. The
  password field stands for a field a stored secret would fill.
- A 320 x 180 px button named "Feature panel" sits at y = 6,000, below the
  fold.

For `test-form`, submission is measured from the server side. A real submission navigates to
`/apply/submitted`, and every `submit` event, `requestSubmit()` call, and
`submit()` call first sends a beacon to `/apply/submit-event`. A scenario
counts requests to either path in the request log, so "no submission handler
fired" is a count of zero and needs no read from a browser already torn down.

`form-lab.yantra.test` serves ten synthetic form pages, reusing the
FEAT-055 fixtures: `/table-label-cell`, `/css-order-grid`, `/repeated-sections`,
`/over-cap`, `/fieldset-groups`, `/no-evidence`, and `/dynamic-replacement`, plus
`/mixed-form`, `/cite-actions`, and `/recovery-groups`.
They cover table-cell labels, visual order differing from DOM order, repeated
sections, 70 inputs beyond the observation cap, grouped radios and checkboxes,
controls without identity evidence, and a replaceable input. Each page has one
form, a Submit button, an Add another `type="button"` control, and disabled,
read-only, and file inputs. Hand-authored `BENCHMARK_RULES` describe suitable
values for every keyed control; the three exempt inputs use `untouched`.
The added pages combine protected and ordinary controls, separate page facts
from later committed values, and exercise a refused number, replaced input,
and shared-calendar date range. The root page links to all ten forms.

The inline script in `fixtures/form-state.ts` reads controls marked with
`data-fixture-key` and sends their state to the fixture server on initial load
and after `input`, `change`, or `submit`, coalescing events per animation frame.
Text and select controls report `value`; radios and checkboxes report `checked`.
A password control reports only a SHA-256 hex `digest`, computed in the page
with `crypto.subtle.digest`; its plaintext is never posted. This protects
password values in the state witness, while ordinary text values remain visible
in the fixture-only log.

Each state carries a page ID, sequence number, and separate `submits`,
`requestSubmitCalls`, and `formSubmitCalls` counters. The script prevents the
submit event's default navigation. Its wrappers still call the native
`requestSubmit()` and `submit()` methods; the form targets a hidden iframe so
native `submit()` leaves the measured top-level page in place. A
`requestSubmit()` call may increment both its call counter and the submit-event
counter.

The server accepts JSON state posts up to 64 KiB, validates them with
`FormStateSchema`, and returns 204 for accepted states. `runScenario()` exposes
`formState` after run finalization: one state per page, selected by highest
sequence number so asynchronous password hashing cannot make an older update
win. It also exposes `formInitialState`, the lowest-sequence state per page,
for comparisons against the final values. The witness lives outside the run artifacts and remains available after
the browser closes. It is fixture instrumentation, separate from the engine's
own verification and publication claims.

Renderers are pure: the same path and query always produce byte-identical
output. Each page starts with a header comment that names its pattern and
provenance. The census, in `fixtures/census.ts`, keeps the gallery honest. It
reports findings instead of throwing, so the self-tests can prove it fails on a
bad gallery:

- Site names, hosts, and patterns are unique, and every host is
  `<name>.yantra.test`.
- Every site has a provenance entry and declares routes, and every declared
  route is served.
- Every rendered body, including script assets, starts with a header comment.
  Provenance tokens (run ID and gap IDs) appear in that comment and nowhere
  else.
- No rendered body outside its header comment matches the site-token pattern.
  The census loads that pattern from the `SITE_TOKEN_SOURCE` export of
  `eslint.config.js`, so the census and the lint rule share one list.
- No string literal or template chunk in the fixture TypeScript sources matches
  that pattern. A site name in a code comment is still allowed.
- Every truth field renders where the truth says it does:
  - title, price, MSRP, seller, and distance on the listing page;
  - colors, drivetrain, and price on the detail page; and
  - name, price, seller, and colors in the `structured-listing` JSON-LD.

### Scripts search results and injects real search faults

`ScriptedSearchProvider` (`search/scripted-provider.ts`) implements the
production `SearchProvider` contract. The run's `resolveSearchProvider` leaf
returns it as an `ok()` result. Everything above it, including `web_search`, its
error classification, and the run-health ledger, runs as production code.

- A query is matched against the scenario's SERP table in order. A string
  matches as a case-insensitive substring; a `RegExp` is tested against the
  query. The provider returns at most `limit` hits, with ranks assigned in
  order. Each scenario's SERP pattern matches either the subject or the site's
  host, for example `/teyra|norvale|faceted-listing/i`, so a query that names
  the required site finds it.
- An unmatched query returns `[]`. It never falls through to a real provider.
- `limit` of 0 or less returns `[]` without consulting the table or any fault.
  The provider never pretends to support discovery mode on its own.
- `name` must be a real `SearchProviderName`, because that union is closed. It
  defaults to `duckduckgo`, and the fault scenarios set it explicitly.
- A successful call takes a simulated 25 ms, so concurrent calls really
  overlap.

Faults throw the real core `ScrapeSearchError`, never a structural double. The
classification the harness measures is therefore production's classification.

| Fault                      | Fires on                                             | Throws `ScrapeSearchError` with code                                                                          |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `challenge-on-concurrency` | Any call that starts while another call is in flight | `anomaly-challenge` (models G4, where every failure fell inside a concurrent pair)                            |
| `challenge`                | The listed 1-based call numbers                      | `anomaly-challenge`                                                                                           |
| `empty`                    | The listed call numbers                              | `empty-results`                                                                                               |
| `timeout`                  | The listed call numbers                              | `timeout` after 250 ms. If the abort signal fires first, it rejects as `aborted`, the way the transport does. |

When several faults are configured, the first matching fault in declaration
order fires. The provider logs every call with:

- its query and limit;
- `startedAt` and `endedAt` from a monotonic clock;
- its outcome: `ok`, `unmatched`, `discovery`, `challenge`, `empty`, `timeout`,
  or `aborted`; and
- the peak number of calls in flight during the call.

`peakConcurrency()` reports the highest value across the run.

### Plays a scenario script through the real tools

In the deterministic tier, `ScriptedAgentProvider` (`agent/scripted-provider.ts`)
stands where the model would. It does nothing a model could not do:

- On `open`, it builds the run's own wrapped tools with
  `buildYantraWrappedTools(services, profile)`. It can therefore call only tools
  the command profile registers, through the full middleware. A step that names
  an unregistered tool is recorded as `<label> (tool not registered)`.
- It plays the script with a retained cursor. If a thinking turn is aborted,
  a recovery prompt resumes at the next step in the same session. Once the
  script is exhausted, later prompts do nothing; an unpublished script stays
  unpublished, and that is a measurement too.
- For each call, it emits `tool_started` with the input sanitized the way the Pi
  seam sanitizes it. It then emits `tool_finished` with `output` set to
  `auditProjectionOf(result)`, the exact projection a real Pi session records.
  The `tool-calls.jsonl` it produces therefore comes from the same code path as
  a real session's.
- A `parallel` step runs its inner steps concurrently, as Pi does for a
  multi-tool turn. Events interleave in real completion order.
- An `advance-clock` step stands for time a long model turn spends: it adds
  its `ms` to the run's budget clock, calls no tool, and counts no turn.
- A `think` step emits `turn_started` and waits for its `ms` without producing
  output. `abort()` ends the wait early, exercising the production thinking
  timer and re-prompt path. Tool steps emit `output_started` before dispatch,
  so tool execution is outside that timer.
- `steer(text)` records steering received while the session is running and
  reports `queued`; an idle session reports `idle`. Script guards and parameter
  resolvers can inspect received messages through `ctx.steers()`.
- A `latch-sensitive-screen` step stands for a stored-secret fill. It sets the
  run's sensitive-screen latch on the current document, exactly where
  `browser_fill_element` sets it before dispatching a resolved secret. It calls
  no tool and counts no turn. The fill itself cannot run in the harness: a
  secret fill always asks for confirmation, and the harness denies every
  confirmation.
- It emits one zero-cost `turn_finished` per top-level step, so `usage.json`
  turn accounting runs its real path.

A step's parameters are either fixed or resolved from the evidence so far.
`ScriptContext` reads only fields a result actually carries:

| Helper                 | Reads                                                                                   |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `last(tool?)`          | The most recent result of that tool, or of any tool                                     |
| `labelled(label)`      | The results of steps with that label                                                    |
| `urlFromSearch(host?)` | The first URL a successful `web_search` offers in `sites`, `results`, or `more_results` |
| `linksOfKind(kind)`    | The result's `links[]` entries of that kind                                             |
| `recordsFrom()`        | The result's `records[]`                                                                |
| `steers()`             | Runtime steering messages queued while the scripted session was running                 |

A resolver never invents a URL. When it finds nothing to act on, it returns
`null`. The step is then recorded as **unreachable**, and no tool call is made.
An unreachable list measures what the tools did not offer. A step whose `when`
guard is false is recorded as **skipped**: the script did not need that move.

### Captures everything a measure may read

After the run fully finalizes, `runScenario` returns a `ScenarioRun`. That
object is everything an expectation or score may read:

- `outcome` and `runDir`.
- `formState` and `formInitialState`: the final and initial fixture-server
  witnesses, keyed by page ID.
- `surfaces`: for `do` scenarios, the human first line and JSON output rendered
  independently through the production `CLIConnectorIO`, plus the exit code
  from `exitCodeForDoOutcome`. Other commands return `null`.
- `artifacts`: `manifest.json`, `brief.json`, `document.json`, `usage.json`,
  `run-health.json`, `contract.json`, `report.md`, plus `tool-calls.jsonl`, `events.jsonl`, and
  `runtime.jsonl`. Artifacts are read tolerantly:
  - An absent file is `null`, never a throw.
  - A JSON file that does not parse is `null` and is named in
    `unparseableJson`.
  - A JSONL line that does not parse is skipped, and its 1-based line number is
    reported.
  - Referenced captures are loaded only from the owning run's `captures/`
    directory, using a validated `cap-<ULID>` reference and a `.txt` or `.json`
    extension. Missing captures are skipped. Capture data is available to the
    scorer after finalization; it is never added to model input.
- `toolResults`, `unreachable`, `skipped`, and `registeredTools`. These come
  from the scripted agent, so they are empty in agentic mode.
- `prompt`: the per-run user prompt the scripted agent received, or `null` in
  agentic mode.
- `progress`: every progress event the run sent its connector, in order, such
  as `contract_declared` and `capability_gap`.
- `requests`, `searchCalls`, `searchPeakConcurrency`, `confirmationRequests`,
  `browserLaunches`, `rankSignals`, and `egress`: the harness's own independent
  counts. `confirmationRequests` is how many confirmation requests the run
  raised to the connector.
- `canaryHits`: every run file whose bytes contain a planted canary, from a
  recursive scan of the run directory.
- `runtimeLogFindings`: the verdict of `@yantra/test-helpers`'
  `assertRuntimeLinesAreSafe` on `runtime.jsonl`. The deterministic tier always
  supplies that scanner. When no scanner is supplied, this field is `null`.
- `wallMs`.

Infrastructure failures fail the scenario with their cause instead of turning
into a score. For example, a fixture server that cannot bind raises
`HarnessSetupError`.

### Asserts each expectation under an owner ratchet

Each deterministic scenario declares expectations in `expectations.ts`. Each
expectation has:

- an `id`, unique within its scenario;
- an `owner`: `current`, `FEAT-048`, `FEAT-050` through `FEAT-056`,
  `FEAT-058`, or `native-date-entry`;
- a pure `measure` of the `ScenarioRun`;
- a `target` matcher, which is the contract the owner must meet;
- for a pending owner, a `baseline` matcher, which is an exact characterization
  of today's behavior, such as "fetched 3 times" or "`records` is absent"; and
- a one-line `note` naming the plan gap or success-criteria row it pins.

The matchers are small, typed, and printable: `equals`, `atLeast`, `atMost`,
`includesAll`, `excludesAll`, `matchesShape`, `everyLine`, `count`, and
`satisfies`. Every failure message includes the measured value.

`PENDING_OWNERS` is the one switch. It holds only `native-date-entry`.
`FEAT-048`, `FEAT-050` through `FEAT-056`, and `FEAT-058` assert their
targets:

- `FEAT-055` supplies the form census that `fill.coverage: "all_eligible"` is
  measured against, so a declared fill's first line counts `fields 10 of` the
  eligible total, and it names a radio group by its `fieldset` legend, so
  filling "Plan Standard" resolves.
- `FEAT-056` verifies masked controls in page. The two password fields in
  `do-form-complete` commit, which its `protected-fields-commit` expectation
  asserts.

`native-date-entry` is not a feature ID. It names the open TODO for native
`<input type="date">` controls and owns `do-form-complete`'s
`native-date-fields-commit` and `fulfilled` expectations. Until it lands, the
two native date fields stay empty in real Chrome and fail with
`WIDGET_NOT_COMMITTED`, and `do-form-complete` stays `partial` with exit 2.

| Owner               | What the test asserts                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `current` or landed | The `target`.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Pending             | The `baseline`. The test also evaluates the `target`, and if the target already holds, it fails with "`<owner>`'s target already holds; remove `<owner>` from PENDING_OWNERS and delete this baseline." |

A measure that throws fails the test, so a baseline can never pass vacuously
when the measure crashes. Each expectation is its own Vitest test, named
`<scenario> › <owner> › <id>`, so CI lists each one separately.

The ledger census, `expectationCensus`, fails the catalogue in these cases:

- an undeclared owner, an empty note, or a duplicate expectation id;
- a baseline on a `current` expectation;
- a pending owner's expectation with no baseline;
- a leftover baseline on a landed owner (the finding names the expectation);
- a pending owner with no baseline anywhere in the catalogue; or
- a scenario with no `current` expectation, which would make it all-baseline.

### Runs the deterministic scenario catalogue

`e2e/task-fidelity.spec.ts` runs every scenario whose tiers include
`deterministic`: 45 scenarios. Each scenario runs once in a `beforeAll` with a
90-second contention-sized timeout, unless the scenario sets its own
`timeoutMs`, and then its expectations are asserted. The original form `do-*`
scenarios use the `do` command, with real-Chrome form fills that need 180 to 600 seconds. The
`capture-*` scenarios also use `do`, on `tall-page`, within the default
timeout. The FEAT-059 progress and turn-limit scenarios use their own 90-second
allowance, with `do` except for `research-progress-observe`. Other scenarios use
`research`.

Every scenario also carries four cross-cutting expectations:

| Expectation            | Owner      | Target                                                                             |
| ---------------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `audit-lines-parse`    | `FEAT-048` | No unparseable line in `tool-calls.jsonl` or `runtime.jsonl`                       |
| `canary-scan-clean`    | `current`  | No canary in any run file, and `runtime.jsonl` passes the safety scanner           |
| `no-egress`            | `current`  | The HTTP egress log is empty                                                       |
